sections.title: How does the Perimeter of a quadrilateral calculator work?
sections.html:
The Perimeter of a quadrilateral calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports side (d) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the side (a), the side (b), the side (c) and the perimeter.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Perimeter of a quadrilateral calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Side (d)=-side (a) − side (b) − side (c) + perimeter
Y₂=Y₁ + the square root of ((side (a) − X₁ + X₂) × (side (a) + X₁ − X₂))
Y₄=Y₁ + the square root of ((side (b) − X₁ + X₄) × (side (b) + X₁ − X₄))
Y₂=Y₃ + the square root of ((side (c) − X₂ + X₃) × (side (c) + X₂ − X₃))
Y₄=Y₃ + the square root of ((side (d) − X₃ + X₄) × (side (d) + X₃ − X₄))
Perimeter=side (a) + side (b) + side (c) + side (d)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.html:

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Side (d) = -60 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Given set to 4 sides and Side (a) = 30 cm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Perimeter of a quadrilateral calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the side and the perimeter — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Perimeter of a quadrilateral calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns side (d), derived from the side and the perimeter. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Perimeter of a quadrilateral calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the side and the perimeter, which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter side (a) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Side (a) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Side (d) = -60 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Perimeter of a quadrilateral calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
